title: Launched Thefacebook from a Harvard dorm room
statement: Zuckerberg launched Thefacebook on February 4, 2004, with roommates Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes, six days after Harvard seniors Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss and Divya Narendra accused him of stalling their HarvardConnection project while building a competing product.
outcome: The service expanded from Harvard to Columbia, New York University, Stanford, and the Ivy League within months; Zuckerberg dropped out and moved the team to Palo Alto that summer, where Peter Thiel made the company's first outside investment.

title: Raised a $12.7 million Series A from Accel at a $98 million valuation
statement: In April 2005, Accel Partners invested $12.7 million at a $98 million valuation, a round that put Accel's Jim Breyer on a five-seat board alongside Zuckerberg and Peter Thiel while leaving two seats open for the founder to nominate.
outcome: The founder retained effective control of the company he had built in a semester while funding campus expansion; Facebook bought the Facebook.com domain and dropped the definite article from its name that same year.

title: Launched the News Feed over mass user protest
statement: Facebook introduced the News Feed on September 5, 2006, concentrating friends' updates into a single stream; roughly a million of the service's eight million users joined protest groups, and a Students Against Facebook group gathered nearly 300,000 members in two days over the lack of privacy controls or an opt-out.
outcome: Zuckerberg apologized on the company blog and conceded the team had not built proper privacy controls, but declined to withdraw the product; the feed became the engine of Facebook's engagement and, eventually, its advertising business.

title: Acquired Instagram weeks before the IPO
statement: Facebook agreed on April 9, 2012, to acquire Instagram for approximately $1 billion in cash and stock, days after the photo app's Android release drew more than a million downloads in a single day and six weeks before Facebook's own public offering.
outcome: The deal closed that September for $300 million in cash plus 23 million shares after the FTC closed its investigation; Instagram grew into Meta's second flagship consumer platform, and the purchase became the recurring exhibit in a decade of antitrust argument.

title: Took Facebook public at $38 a share with majority voting control
statement: Facebook priced its initial public offering at $38, the top of its range, valuing the company at $104 billion, the largest valuation for a newly public company at the time, with Zuckerberg retaining twenty-two percent ownership and fifty-seven percent of the voting shares under the dual-class structure instituted in 2009.
outcome: Nasdaq's opening malfunction delayed trading and left firms with losses; the stock closed its first day at $38.23, traded at $26.81 a week later, and drew more than forty lawsuits before recovering as mobile advertising scaled.

title: Acquired WhatsApp for $19 billion
statement: Facebook agreed to acquire WhatsApp for $19 billion, then the largest acquisition of a venture-backed company in history, paying $4 billion in cash, $12 billion in stock, and $3 billion in restricted units binding founders Jan Koum and Brian Acton, with the decision informed by usage signals from Facebook's Onavo analytics app.
outcome: Sequoia's stake returned roughly 5,000 percent; some users migrated to Telegram and Line on announcement, but WhatsApp grew into the world's most popular messenger, with three billion monthly users by 2025 as the messaging layer of Meta's portfolio.

title: Testified before Congress after the Cambridge Analytica revelations
statement: After whistleblower reporting revealed that a personality-quiz app had harvested data from up to 87 million Facebook profiles for Cambridge Analytica's political targeting, Zuckerberg testified for more than four hours before a joint Senate Judiciary and Commerce hearing, apologizing and taking personal responsibility for not doing enough to prevent the platform's misuse.
outcome: The Federal Trade Commission fined Facebook $5 billion in July 2019 and the UK Information Commissioner's Office added a 500,000 pound penalty; the stock recovered its losses within two months, and Zuckerberg announced a privacy-focused pivot to encrypted messaging within a year.

title: Announced a privacy-focused vision for social networking
statement: Zuckerberg published a privacy-focused vision for social networking built on six principles: private interactions, end-to-end encryption that excludes even Facebook itself, reducing permanence, safety, interoperability across Messenger, WhatsApp, and Instagram, and secure data storage outside countries with weak human-rights records.
outcome: The vision repositioned the company around private messaging and interoperable apps, framing the strategic redirection that Zuckerberg presented as the answer to the post-Cambridge Analytica environment.

title: Rebranded the company as Meta around the metaverse
statement: At the Connect conference on October 28, 2021, Zuckerberg renamed the parent company Meta Platforms and committed its future to the metaverse, announcing separate reporting for Family of Apps and Reality Labs beginning with fourth-quarter 2021 results and a new MVRS stock ticker.
outcome: Reality Labs posted a $13.72 billion operating loss in 2022 and Meta lost almost two-thirds of its market value that year, but Zuckerberg defended the spending as the platform bet for the next computing era.

title: Declared the year of efficiency and cut roughly 21,000 roles
statement: After laying off 11,000 employees in November 2022 and admitting he had wrongly predicted that the pandemic e-commerce surge would persist, Zuckerberg announced the year of efficiency: a further reduction of about 10,000 roles plus 5,000 unfilled open positions, flatter organizations with fewer management layers, and the cancellation of lower-priority projects.
outcome: Meta's shares finished 2023 up 150 percent and reached an all-time high in January 2024, as cost discipline coincided with the Llama 2 release and an AI-led investment narrative.

title: Released Llama 3.1 405B as the first frontier-level open source model
statement: Zuckerberg released Llama 3.1 405B, which he presented as the first frontier-level open source AI model, accompanied by a manifesto arguing that open source AI would follow Linux's path to becoming the industry standard, and that Meta, which does not sell model access, sacrifices no revenue by giving the weights away.
outcome: The release anchored an ecosystem spanning Amazon, Databricks, NVIDIA, Groq, and the AWS, Azure, Google, and Oracle clouds, positioning Llama as the open alternative to closed frontier models from OpenAI and Google.
